sections.title: Kosem Kesamim (Practising Divination)
sections.html:
Kosem kesamim (one who practises divination) is one of the prohibitions of sorcery, as it is stated (Devarim 18:9-13): "When you come into the land that the Lord your God is giving you, you shall not learn to do according to the abominations of those nations. There shall not be found among you anyone who passes his son or his daughter through the fire, one who practises divination, a soothsayer, a diviner of omens, or a sorcerer… For whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord, and because of these abominations the Lord your God is driving them out from before you. You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God." One who transgresses the prohibition and practises divination is liable to lashes.

The aim of the diviner (kosem) is to know the future. To this end he would perform various acts by means of which he disconnected himself from his surroundings and from his bodily sensations and sank into a meditative-hypnotic state of consciousness, while trying to connect with higher powers. From within this state he would guess the future, or decide whether or not it was worthwhile to do a certain thing. Some did this by repeatedly striking with a stick while making strange sounds; some did it by stirring sand while forming various shapes; some made use of stones or sand; some gazed at length into a mirror or into the flame of a lamp; and some bowed down to the ground while making strange movements (see Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:6; Sefer Ha-ḥinukh 510).

There were people who made use of divination without going to an expert diviner. In one widespread form of divination, they would take a branch and peel one side of it; the side with the bark they called "man," and the peeled side "woman." If they wished to set out on a journey, they would throw the stick twice: if "man" came up first and then "woman," they decided that the journey was good and set out. If "woman" came up and then "man," they decided that the journey was not good and did not set out. And if "man" came up twice or "woman" twice, they said it was an "average journey." Concerning this the prophet rebuked them (Hoshe'a 4:12): "My people consults its piece of wood, and its staff declares to it; for a spirit of harlotry has led them astray, and they have strayed from under their God" (SMaG, negative commandment 52; Bekhor Shor and Hadar Zekenim on Devarim 18:10).

One of the famous diviners was Bil'am, who, in addition to his ability to curse by his sorcery, would foretell the future through his divinations. Therefore, when Balak wished to harm Israel, he sent messengers to Bil'am with instruments of divination, as it is stated: "And the elders of Moav and the elders of Midyan went with divinations in their hand" (Bamidbar 22:7; Rashi). This was because he feared that Bil'am might be afraid to curse Israel, and so that Bil'am could not evade his messengers on the pretext that he had no instruments of divination, he placed instruments of divination in their hands, by means of which Bil'am could determine the right time to curse them (Ibn Ezra). In the end, however, the Lord turned his curse into a blessing, and the Children of Israel took their vengeance on him, as it is stated (Yehoshua 13:22): "And Bil'am the son of Be'or, the diviner, the Children of Israel slew with the sword among the rest of their slain."

One who seeks the counsel of a diviner also transgresses a prohibition, for he neglects the positive commandment by which the Torah commanded Israel to conduct themselves with wholeheartedness, as it is stated (Devarim 18:13): "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God." That is, to believe that the Lord watches over man and that all His governance is for man's good; therefore one must not try to know the future by the crooked ways of divination and tricks (above 19:12-13). However, the diviner, who performs the divination himself, also transgresses a negative prohibition (lav). And some say that one who consults a diviner also transgresses a negative prohibition.1

sections.title: Me'onen (Soothsayer)
sections.html:
Included in the prohibitions of sorcery are the me'onen (soothsayer) and the menaḥesh (diviner of omens), as it is stated (Devarim 18:10): "There shall not be found among you anyone who passes his son or his daughter through the fire, one who practises divination, a soothsayer, or a diviner of omens." It is likewise stated (Vayikra 19:26): "You shall not eat over the blood; you shall not practise divination by omens, nor practise soothsaying." A me'onen is one who believes the sorcerers that there are good times and bad times, as will be explained further on in this halakha. A menaḥesh is one who believes that he can know, on the basis of events that happened to him by chance, what it is worthwhile for him to do, as will be explained in the next halakha.

In general, the superstitions of the me'onen and the menaḥesh were created by people with mystical intuition who engaged in sorcery and divination and sensed that certain things hint at danger or at success. Sometimes the divination was based on a natural feeling. For example, a person who began his business day by paying a high tax might become depressed and as a result fail in his business that day; the diviners concluded that paying a tax at the beginning of the day causes mystical forces to plot against him, and they therefore instructed people to avoid paying tax at the beginning of the day, the week or the month. Israel, however, are commanded to direct their faith to the Torah and the mitzvot, which elevate a person to do good deeds and to add blessing to the world, and not to turn to superstitions that have no rational basis.

Even when it appears that sometimes the sorcerers who engaged in divination succeeded in guessing the future, in truth they did not see the whole picture. Consequently, even if one who followed them gained in the short term, in the long term he lost twice over. First, relying on the instructions of sorcerers prevents a person from weighing rational considerations, from which more blessing grows for him. Second, one who follows them focuses all his attention, including his spiritual attention, on external success alone, and removes himself from the Torah, whose guidance is intended to elevate a person morally and to add blessing to his life in this world and in the World to Come.

Who is a me'onen? Rabbi Akiva explained: "This is one who calculates times and hours, and says: Today is a good day to set out; tomorrow is a good day to buy (merchandise); the wheat of the eve of the Sabbatical years is fine (wheat that grows on the eve of the Shemita year tends to be fine)." Me'onen derives from the word ona (a time or season), and one who sins in this way acts according to a superstition that certain times are good and certain times are bad (Sanhedrin 65b). Whoever performs an action on this basis is liable to lashes (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:9).

However, there is no prohibition in guidance of the Sages concerning times that is based on Torah values. Thus the Sages advised (Ta'anit 29b) a Jew who has a lawsuit with a gentile to avoid it during the month of Av, when his fortune (mazal) is bad, and to try to make himself available for the lawsuit or for business in the month of Adar, when the fortune of Israel is successful.2

sections.title: Menaḥesh (Diviner of Omens)
sections.html:
Menaḥesh derives from the word "to hasten" (Ramban). Naturally, a person does not know what will happen in the future until it actually happens, and the menaḥesh wants to hasten and know the future on the basis of events that are happening to him now, without there being any rational causal connection between what happened to him and what he guesses will be. The Sages brought examples (Sanhedrin 65b) of things forbidden under the prohibition of menaḥesh: "One who says: his bread fell from his mouth" – and on this basis worries about harm all that day. Likewise if "his staff fell from his hand, his son calls him from behind, a raven calls to him, a deer cut across his path, a snake was on his right and a fox on his left," and he saw in this a bad sign, and on that basis refrained from setting out on a journey or from doing business as he had planned. Likewise "those who divine by means of a weasel, birds, fish and stars" transgress the prohibition of divining omens (Sanhedrin 66a). That is, there was a superstition that if a person saw certain things in birds, fish or stars, it would be a sign for him to do the business or set out on the journey, or to refrain from doing so.

There was likewise a superstition that one who pays the customs duty at the beginning of the day, or at the beginning of the month or of the week, will lose in his business. Therefore, when the tax collector comes to collect taxes, one who says to him: "Do not start with me, (for) it is morning, it is Rosh Ḥodesh, it is Motza'ei Shabbat," transgresses the prohibition of divining omens (Sanhedrin 66a).

Similarly, included in the prohibition of divining omens, it is forbidden to perform acts based on superstitions practised by the gentiles. For example, those who believe that if a hen crows with the voice of a rooster it is a bad sign, and to be saved from it one must slaughter the hen. Likewise, people who raised chicks used to dash eggs against a wall as a charm (segula) for the chicks' survival, and there were women who for this purpose danced before the chicks and counted seventy-one of them. There were also customs of women connected to cooking food: when they prepared a kutaḥ dish, they danced before the dish so that it would turn out well; when they cooked lentils they silenced people so that they would not spoil the cooking; and when they cooked groats they shrieked so that they would cook well (Shabbat 67b).

Similarly, some fear a black cat that has passed in front of them, regarding it as a bad sign, and change their plans as a result. Some are afraid to go back into a house they have just left, and if they forgot something, they walk around a little and only then return home. Some are afraid to whistle at home, out of concern that the whistling will cause there to be no money in the house. Some avoid sitting at the corner of the table, lest whoever sits there not marry for seven years. Some avoid stepping over a baby or a child out of concern that his development will be harmed, and some are very careful not to break a mirror. And some wear a red thread as a charm. Whoever fears things such as these transgresses the prohibition of divining omens.

Some hold, however, that any custom that God-fearing Jews also feared is permitted. For example, it is permitted for one who has left the house to avoid going back into it out of fear of danger, and it is permitted to avoid stepping over a baby. In practice, however, it seems that since these are customs learned from the gentiles, and they have no rational basis, they are forbidden. True, in the past there were those who feared customs of this sort that were learned from the gentiles, but that was because they thought that they truly involved an occult (segulit) danger; today, however, when many know that they involve no danger, the law has reverted to its place, and they are forbidden because of divining omens. This is the rule: whoever performs an action or refrains from performing an action on the basis of superstitions transgresses the prohibition of divining omens.3

sections.title: Divining Omens Is Forbidden, a Sign Is Permitted
sections.html:
The Sages said: although divining omens (niḥush) is forbidden, a sign (siman) is permitted (Ḥullin 95b). For example, a person who bought a house, married a wife or had a child born to him, and since then succeeded in his business three times, may see this as a good sign that he has entered a good period of success, and be encouraged to increase his business dealings. Conversely, if since then he lost in his business three times, he may see this as a bad sign that this period is not successful for him, and that he would do better to reduce his business dealings.

But all this is on condition that he treats the sign as a possibility that may perhaps materialise, and not as a forecast that he believes will materialise, so that his main consideration will be according to reason and not according to the sign. Thus, if by his understanding the deal he is interested in making is good, he will not refrain from making it even if he had a bad sign, and likewise the reverse. For one may make use of a sign as an indication of direction that joins the main consideration; but if he treats the sign as a forecast that he believes will materialise, the sign will become the main reason for his doing business or refraining from it, and he will transgress the prohibition of menaḥesh.

That is to say, events that have happened to a person contain a sign and an expression of a certain atmosphere in which he finds himself, positive or negative, and one may pay attention to this. But the diviners of omens exaggerated the importance of signs and conducted their lives according to them, and thereby transgressed the prohibition of divining omens. All the more so, it is forbidden to act according to signs when taking them into account will harm the values of the Torah and its mitzvot.4

Since signs have a certain value in creating a positive atmosphere that influences life for the good, the Sages recommended eating foods on Rosh Ha-shana that express a good sign for the whole year (Horayot 12a; SA OḤ 583:1-2; Peninei Halakha, Yamim Nora'im 3:12). Likewise, it is customary to say verses of blessing at Havdala as a good sign, and many are accustomed to fill the Havdala cup until it overflows, so that a little wine spills as a good sign of abundance (Rema OḤ 296:1). Similarly, it was the custom to anoint kings of the House of David beside a spring, as a sign of blessing that their kingship would continue (Horayot 12a). Similarly, those of Ashkenazi communities were accustomed to hold wedding canopies (ḥuppot) under the open sky, as a sign of blessing that their offspring would multiply like the stars of the heavens (Rema EH 61:1). Likewise, some were accustomed to begin studying a new tractate on Rosh Ḥodesh, as a good sign of renewal (Rema YD 179:2). But one must not neglect Torah study because of this custom (Sefer Ḥasidim 59).

Some were accustomed to schedule weddings in the first half of the month, on the days when the moon is waxing, and not in the second half of the month, when the moon is waning. Most of Israel, however, were not particular about this, for the rule is that one should not change plans or harm values because of signs, and avoiding scheduling weddings in the second half of the month could cause the mitzva of marriage to be postponed by several days and add to the costs.5

sections.title: Is Divining by a Future Sign Forbidden? (Eliezer and Yehonatan)
sections.html:
Some say that there is no prohibition in setting a sign such that if it happens, one will carry out one's plan, and if not, one will abandon it, while believing that in this way one will succeed. For in their view the prohibition of divining omens is to act according to a sign that has already occurred, such as a deer that crossed one's path, so that one therefore decided not to set out on one's journey; but setting a sign for the future is permitted (Ra'avad). And although it is proper for a person to make his decisions according to reason and not according to random signs, this involves no prohibition of divining omens.

According to most of the Rishonim, however, just as it is forbidden to divine according to an incident that happened to a person, such as his bread falling or a fox passing on his left, while believing that if he acts according to these signs he will succeed in his path, so it is forbidden to divine according to a sign that he sets for himself in advance, while believing that in this way he will succeed in his business. For example, he sets for himself that if someone at a meeting wears a blue garment, he will agree to the deal, and if not, he will refuse it. That is, the rule in the prohibition of divining omens is that a person may not decide how to act according to random signs while believing that in this way he will succeed. Since this is the opinion of most of the Rishonim, and moreover this is a dispute concerning a Torah prohibition, this is how the halakha is ruled.

But if the sign one set for the future has a certain logic to it, even according to the stringent view there is no prohibition of divining omens. Thus did Eliezer, the servant of Avraham, who set for himself a sign that the young woman who would volunteer to take the trouble to give drink to him and his camels would be the woman whom "the Lord has appointed" as suitable for Yitzḥak, since this sign testifies to her goodness of heart. And although there is no prohibition in such a sign, it is not proper to act according to signs of this kind, as the Sages said (Ta'anit 4a) that Eliezer "asked improperly," for had an unsuitable young woman volunteered to give him drink, according to the sign he would have been obligated to match her with Yitzḥak. Therefore, although one may set a sign that has logic to it, it is right to set it as a sign from which one draws inspiration, and not as a sign on which one relies.6

According to all opinions there is no prohibition for one who finds it difficult to decide to set for himself a decision mechanism according to which he will act, such as deciding to act according to the toss of a coin. And although one who acts this way is not acting wisely, since he does not hold that the coin will predict his success, there is no prohibition of divining omens in this.7

sections.title: Asking a Child for a Verse
sections.html:
There were Sages who, when they were uncertain whether to set out on a journey or to do something, would ask a small child who was studying Scripture: "Tell me your verse." That is, tell me the verse you learned today; and from the verse he said, they resolved their doubt. Likewise it is told of Rabbi Yoḥanan, who lived in the Land of Israel and was uncertain whether to go down to Babylonia to meet the Amora Shmuel, that in order to resolve his doubt he asked a child what verse he had learned. The child answered: "And Shmuel died, and all Israel lamented him" (I Shmuel 28:3). Rabbi Yoḥanan concluded from this that Shmuel had passed away, and he remained in the Land. The Gemara concludes, however, that in truth Shmuel was alive, but so that Rabbi Yoḥanan would not trouble himself to go down to Babylonia, this verse was arranged for him from Heaven (Ḥullin 95b).

The Rishonim explained that this incident involves no prohibition of divining omens, for the prohibition of divining omens is to rely on signs that have no logic to them, whereas asking a child for a verse involves a kind of "minor prophecy." For the Sages said (Bava Batra 12b): "From the day the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to fools and to children" (small children). According to Rambam, however, it is forbidden to act according to what the child says; one may only rejoice if he says a good verse, and take encouragement from the fact that it is a good sign regarding something one has already done (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:5). But according to most poskim, it is permitted to act according to the verse the child says, on condition that the guidance emerging from the verse is not contrary to the guidance of the Torah or to reason. In practice, the vast majority of rabbis throughout all the generations did not customarily make use of "asking for a verse," but rather acted according to their own judgement.8

sections.title: Opening a Book
sections.html:
Just as there were Sages who sometimes resolved a doubt by "asking for a verse," so sometimes they resolved a doubt by opening a Torah scroll and looking at the verse that opened before them. Thus it is told in the Talmud (Ḥullin 95b) of the Amora Shmuel, that sometimes when he was uncertain, he would open a book to see what verse would come to him. As with asking for a verse, according to Rambam (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:5) it is forbidden to act according to this; one may only rejoice if he sees a good verse, and take encouragement from the fact that it is a good sign regarding something he has already done. According to most poskim, however, it is permitted to act according to the verse that came up before him, on condition that the guidance emerging from it is not contrary to the guidance of the Torah or to reason.9

In recent generations, there were rabbis who used a sophisticated method of opening a book, called the "Goral Ha-Gra" (the lottery of the Vilna Gaon). According to it, one opens a Torah scroll or a Tanakh at random, counts seven pages from the place of opening, and looks at the eighth page, in the eighth line, at the eighth letter, and there one looks for an answer or a hint of an answer. It seems, however, that this method does not originate with the Gra, for none of his disciples mentioned it, and only several generations later was it mentioned in his name.

In practice, it is preferable not to use opening a book to make decisions, including the method called "Goral Ha-Gra." First, the vast majority of rabbis of all generations did not make use of "opening a book" or "asking for a verse," but weighed their actions in light of the guidance of the Torah as they understood it with their intellect; evidently they held that opening a book is a less good method of decision-making. Second, some say that it is forbidden to make decisions on the basis of opening a book (Rambam and Tur), and although most poskim are lenient, it is proper to be stringent from the outset (le-khatḥila). Only in special cases, when the matter does not concern decisions for the future but is meant to prevent anguish, is there perhaps room to use this method, as Rav Aryeh Levin of blessed memory did in order to set up gravestones for the holy martyrs of the Convoy of the Thirty-Five (Shayeret Ha-Lamed-Heh), who were killed in the war for the defence of the people and the Land.10

sections.title: Lotteries, Tarot Cards and Coffee Reading
sections.html:
It is forbidden to use a lottery (goral) in order to foretell the future or to advise a person how to act so that he will succeed, as it is stated (Devarim 18:13): "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God" (SA YD 179:1). That is, there are beliefs that by various supernatural means one can foretell the future and thereby be more successful in life, and the Torah commanded us not to follow them, but to rely on the Lord and on the natural talents He has given man. Included in the prohibition is also the use of tarot cards and coffee reading. Moreover, it seems that these things are also forbidden because of the prohibition of kosem or menaḥesh, whose essence is foretelling the future on the basis of performing acts or on the basis of events that happened to a person by chance (as explained above in halakhot 1-3). Let us explain a little about the common forbidden methods:

There are simple lotteries that predict the answer to a single question: whether, in order to succeed, the inquirer should do a certain thing or not. And there are complex lotteries based on astrology, according to which the experts in lotteries ascertain the inquirer's mazal according to the date and hour of his birth, and on that basis cast several lots in order to know things about his character, his future, and the good and bad paths before him. All these lotteries are forbidden by Torah law. True, there were Jewish masters of occult practices (ba'alei segulot) who wrote various lottery methods, and even attributed some of them to great early Sages of Israel, and some people act according to them to this day (see the note). But it is difficult to accept these traditions, since the poskim explained that this involves a Torah prohibition. In addition, it has become clear that many lotteries written in the books of Jewish masters of occult practices had previously been written in the books of Greek, Roman and Arab gentiles, and are rooted in traditions of sorcery.

Similar to lotteries, some use tarot cards, which are shuffled and laid face down on the table; the inquirer chooses one card or several cards at random, and according to the cards he chose, his future is foretold to him or he is advised how to act. All this is out of a belief that the random choice corresponds to the inquirer's fate, and expresses his inner world and what is in store for him in the future.

Coffee reading: in the conception of those who believe in it, when a person drinks a liquid, his spirit mingles with the liquid; and since in his subconscious his spirit knows the future that will come upon him, this knowledge passes into the liquid, and the shape of the stains that the liquid leaves on the cup contains hints of it. According to this belief, this is discernible in any drink that leaves stains, and coffee is used in places where it is common.11

sections.title: The Language of Birds
sections.html:
The Sages said that King Shlomo knew how to understand the speech of birds, and this is what is stated (I Melakhim 5:10): "And Shlomo's wisdom exceeded the wisdom of all the children of the East," who were familiar with the language of birds (Bamidbar Rabba 19:3). They likewise learned from the verse (Kohelet 10:20): "For a bird of the heavens will carry the voice, and a winged creature will tell the matter" – "this is the raven and the wisdom of tayarin" (the language of birds).

Similarly, there were Sages who were expert in the speech of trees, such as Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, of whom it was said that he knew the speech of palm trees (Sukka 28a). These branches of wisdom are based on the assumption that everything that is about to happen in the world is first known in the higher worlds, and there are various hints of this in the world, in the movement of the trees and in the chirping and flight of birds. Maharal explained that precisely animals, which are simpler than man, sometimes receive an impression from the higher realms and express it unwittingly in their own way; and birds, which are more spiritual, perceive more of the future (Netzaḥ Yisrael 26; Ḥiddushei Aggadot, Ḥullin 63a). In the days when mystical powers were more developed, there were those who learned these branches of wisdom (Sefer Ha-gilgulim 35; Shela, parashat Noaḥ, Torah Or).

It is told in the Talmud (Gittin 45a) of Rav Ilish, who was taken captive, and with him in captivity was a gentile who knew how to understand the language of birds. The gentile heard a raven and a dove saying: "Ilish, flee! Ilish, flee!" On this basis Rav Ilish decided to flee and was saved. But the gentile who understood the language of birds and fled with him was caught and killed. And although the Sages said (Sanhedrin 66a) that included in the prohibition of me'onen it is forbidden to divine by means of birds, the meaning is the superstition that if a person sees certain things in birds, this will be a sign for him that it is worthwhile to do business or set out on a journey, or the opposite. But one who truly knows the language of birds is permitted to take it into account (Ritva, Gittin 45a; Nimukei Yosef, Sanhedrin 15b, cited in Beit Yosef).

From Rambam and Ramban, however, it is implied that it is forbidden to perform an action on the basis of the speech of birds, and this prohibition is included in the prohibition of me'onen and menaḥesh (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:4; Ramban, Vayikra 18:19; Maharsha and Ḥida on Sanhedrin 66a). According to their view, Rav Ilish relied on the speech of birds because he was in a situation of mortal danger (pikuaḥ nefesh) (Responsa Rashba 1:413; below 29, note 6).

sections.title: A Magic Show for Entertainment
sections.html:
In recent generations it has become accepted to hold a "magic" show for entertainment, in which the magician makes objects disappear or turns them into other objects, or guesses numbers and facts about people watching the show. The question is whether this involves a prohibition.

According to the stringent view, it is forbidden to perform acts that look like sorcery by means of illusion (aḥizat einayim), even though in practice the "magic" is done by sleight of hand or other methods of deception. This prohibition is included in the prohibition of me'onen, for the Sages said (Sanhedrin 65b) that a me'onen is "one who deceives the eyes." Likewise Abaye said (ibid. 67b), regarding the laws of sorcery: "One who deceives the eyes – is exempt but it is forbidden"; that is, it is forbidden to perform acts of sorcery by means of illusion, but since he did not actually perform sorcery, he is not punished for it with stoning like a sorcerer, or with lashes like a me'onen. According to the stringent view, since it is forbidden to put on a magic show, it is also forbidden to attend one, for whoever attends it helps cause the person performing the magic to stumble (Yeḥaveh Da'at 3:68; Shevet Ha-levi 5:129). However, when the magic show is put on by a gentile, according to most of the stringent authorities it is permitted to attend it, for the prohibition of sorcery applies to Israel and not to gentiles (Yabi'a Omer part 5, YD 14; Avnei Yashfeh part 3, YD 78:6).

Many poskim, however, were lenient regarding putting on a magic show and watching it. Some are lenient on condition that the magician informs his audience that all his acts are by illusion, for the prohibition applies only when people may think that this involves an act of sorcery beyond nature (Divrei Yatziv YD 1:57). And some require that the magician also demonstrate several tricks to the audience, in order to show them that in practice this is indeed sleight of hand and tricks of deception (Si'aḥ Naḥum 53; Ma'aseh Ish part 1, 10:27).

And some hold that there is no need for the magician to inform the audience of this; since everyone knows that he does not use forces of impurity to perform sorcery beyond the laws of nature, but rather his "magic" is done by sleight of hand and sophisticated tricks of deception, there is no prohibition in it. And everything that the Sages said is forbidden to do by illusion applies when the one performing the act claims that it is done by sorcery through supernatural powers (Igrot Moshe YD 4:13; Aseh Lekha Rav 2:44).

In practice, those who wish to be lenient may do so even without the magician needing to announce that his magic is illusion. True, in the past many in the audience believed that this was sorcery performed by supernatural powers, and therefore there was room to be stringent, and at least to require the magician to say that it is illusion. Today, however, it is known that this is not magic performed by supernatural forces of impurity.12
